1.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 10:36. Alternate translation: [Around that time]

1.q: כֹּֽה־אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ צַ֣ו לְ⁠בֵיתֶ֔⁠ךָ כִּ֛י מֵ֥ת אַתָּ֖ה וְ⁠לֹ֥א תִֽחְיֶֽה
1.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that you should command regarding your house, for you are dying, and you will not live]

1.q: צַ֣ו לְ⁠בֵיתֶ֔⁠ךָ כִּ֛י מֵ֥ת אַתָּ֖ה וְ⁠לֹ֥א תִֽחְיֶֽה
1.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since you are dying, and you will not live, command regarding your house]

Here Hezekiah’s **house** could represent: (1) his household affairs. Alternate translation: [Put your affairs in order] or (2) his royal dynasty. Hezekiah lived 15 years after this illness, but his son and successor Manasseh was 12 years old when he became king, indicating that Hezekiah did not have an heir at this time. He would therefore have had to identify someone as his successor. Alternate translation: [Name your successor]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [you will surely die from this illness]

3.note: Hezekiah is not suggesting that Yahweh does not **remember** these things and needs to be reminded of them. He is asking Yahweh to take them into consideration. Alternate translation: [consider] or [take into consideration]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:18. Alternate translation: [I have lived]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:14. Alternate translation: [in your presence]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [faithfully]
Here the **heart** represents a person’s intentions and commitments. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and in complete devotion]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:13. Alternate translation: [and I have done what you consider to be good]

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [And Hezekiah wept bitterly]

4.note: The author is using a common expression of his culture to mean that Yahweh spoke a message to Isaiah. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Samuel 15:10. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh spoke a message to him]

5.q: שׁ֣וּב וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֞ אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֣הוּ נְגִיד־עַמִּ֗⁠י כֹּֽה־אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵי֙ דָּוִ֣ד אָבִ֔י⁠ךָ שָׁמַ֨עְתִּי֙ אֶת־תְּפִלָּתֶ֔⁠ךָ רָאִ֖יתִי אֶת־דִּמְעָתֶ֑⁠ךָ הִנְ⁠נִי֙ רֹ֣פֶא לָ֔⁠ךְ בַּ⁠יּוֹם֙ הַ⁠שְּׁלִישִׁ֔י תַּעֲלֶ֖ה בֵּ֥ית יְהוָֽה
5.note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what Yahweh said (level 1). Yahweh is quoting what he wants Isaiah to say to Hezekiah. (level 2). This includes a quotation from Yahweh himself. (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation, in this verse and at the end of the next verse. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there are not second-level or third-level quotations.

5.q: שׁ֣וּב וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֞ אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֣הוּ נְגִיד־עַמִּ֗⁠י כֹּֽה־אָמַ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵי֙ דָּוִ֣ד אָבִ֔י⁠ךָ שָׁמַ֨עְתִּי֙ אֶת־תְּפִלָּתֶ֔⁠ךָ רָאִ֖יתִי אֶת־דִּמְעָתֶ֑⁠ךָ הִנְ⁠נִי֙ רֹ֣פֶא לָ֔⁠ךְ בַּ⁠יּוֹם֙ הַ⁠שְּׁלִישִׁ֔י תַּעֲלֶ֖ה בֵּ֥ית יְהוָֽה
5.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Return and tell Hezekiah, the leader of my people, that I, Yahweh, the God of David his father, have heard his prayer and have seen his weeping. I am going to heal him. On the third day, he will go up {to} my temple]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:24. Alternate translation: [your ancestor]
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:7. Alternate translation: [I am going to heal you]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:3. Alternate translation: [you will go]

In this culture, the current day was considered the first day, the next day was considered the second day, and the day after that was considered **the third day**. In your translation, describe these days as your language and culture naturally would. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Samuel 30:1. Alternate translation: [On the day after tomorrow]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:18. Alternate translation: [to the temple of Yahweh]

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person because he is making a solemn declaration. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation, as in the UST: [to my temple]

6.q: וְ⁠הֹסַפְתִּ֣י עַל־יָמֶ֗י⁠ךָ חֲמֵ֤שׁ עֶשְׂרֵה֙ שָׁנָ֔ה וּ⁠מִ⁠כַּ֤ף מֶֽלֶךְ־אַשּׁוּר֙ אַצִּ֣ילְ⁠ךָ֔ וְ⁠אֵ֖ת הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֑את וְ⁠גַנּוֹתִי֙ עַל־הָ⁠עִ֣יר הַ⁠זֹּ֔את לְמַֽעֲנִ֔⁠י וּ⁠לְמַ֖עַן דָּוִ֥ד עַבְדִּֽ⁠י
6.note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be quotations within a quotations, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [Tell Hezekiah that I say that I will add 15 years to his days and that I will deliver him and this city from the palm of the king of Assyria. And I will cover over this city for my sake and for the sake of David my servant]
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:36. Alternate translation: [to your lifetime]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:10. Alternate translation: [from the power of the king of Assyria]
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:34. Alternate translation: [And I will protect this city]

8.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 20:5. Alternate translation: [on the day after tomorrow to the temple of Yahweh]

9.note: Since the author explains in verse 11 that these **steps** were the “steps of Ahaz,” that is, a sundial that Hezekiah’s father King Ahaz had built, you do not need to explain here what these steps were.

11.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh made]

The phrase **the steps of Ahaz** describes a structure that King Ahaz, the father of Hezekiah, built to track the passage of time. It showed the time of day by the position of the shadow that a pole cast on a series of **steps** below the pole. Such a structure is sometimes called a “shadow clock.” It is similar to what many cultures know as a sundial. If your readers would not be familiar with such a structure, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [on the steps of the shadow clock that King Ahaz had built] or [on the sundial of King Ahaz]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [The shadow went backward ten steps]

12.note: The author is using the time reference **At that time** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

12.q: שָׁלַ֡ח בְּרֹאדַ֣ךְ בַּ֠לְאֲדָן בֶּֽן־בַּלְאֲדָ֧ן מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֛ל סְפָרִ֥ים וּ⁠מִנְחָ֖ה אֶל־חִזְקִיָּ֑הוּ כִּ֣י שָׁמַ֔ע כִּ֥י חָלָ֖ה חִזְקִיָּֽהוּ
12.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [since Berodach-Baladan, the son of Baladan, the king of Babylon, had heard that Hezekiah was sick, he sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah]

Some ancient manuscripts read “Berodach Baladan.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts and the parallel passage in Isaiah 39:1 read “Merodach Baladan.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:14. Alternate translation: [a letter]
Since the author has already used the name Hezekiah earlier in this sentence, it may be more natural in your language to use a pronoun here. Alternate translation: [that he was sick]

13.note: Some ancient manuscripts read “And Hezekiah listened to them.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts and the parallel passage in Isaiah 39:2 read “And Hezekiah rejoiced over them.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.
See how you translated the similar expression in 12:18. Alternate translation: [and everything that was in his treasuries]

13.q: לֹֽא־הָיָ֣ה דָבָ֗ר אֲ֠שֶׁר לֹֽא־הֶרְאָ֧⁠ם חִזְקִיָּ֛הוּ בְּ⁠בֵית֖⁠וֹ וּ⁠בְ⁠כָל־מֶמְשַׁלְתּֽ⁠וֹ
13.note: This is a double negative, consisting of two instances of the negative particle **not**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [Hezekiah showed them everything in his palace and in his realm]

15.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 20:13. Alternate translation: [I showed them everything in my treasuries]

16.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:7. Alternate translation: [Hear a message from Yahweh]

17.q: הִנֵּה֮ יָמִ֣ים בָּאִים֒ וְ⁠נִשָּׂ֣א ׀ כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּ⁠בֵיתֶ֗⁠ךָ וַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר אָצְר֧וּ אֲבֹתֶ֛י⁠ךָ עַד־הַ⁠יּ֥וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה בָּבֶ֑לָ⁠ה לֹֽא־יִוָּתֵ֥ר דָּבָ֖ר אָמַ֥ר יְהוָֽה
17.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that behold, days are coming when all that is in your house and that your fathers have stored up to this day will be carried away to Babylon. A thing will not be left]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:9.
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:36. Alternate translation: [a time is coming]

17.q: וְ⁠נִשָּׂ֣א ׀ כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּ⁠בֵיתֶ֗⁠ךָ וַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר אָצְר֧וּ אֲבֹתֶ֛י⁠ךָ עַד־הַ⁠יּ֥וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה בָּבֶ֑לָ⁠ה
17.note: The expression **will be carried away** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [when soldiers will carry away to Babylon everything that {is} in your house and that your fathers have stored up to this day]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:24. Alternate translation: [your ancestors]

18.q: וּ⁠מִ⁠בָּנֶ֜י⁠ךָ אֲשֶׁ֨ר יֵצְא֧וּ מִמְּ⁠ךָ֛ אֲשֶׁ֥ר תּוֹלִ֖יד יקח וְ⁠הָיוּ֙ סָֽרִיסִ֔ים בְּ⁠הֵיכַ֖ל מֶ֥לֶךְ בָּבֶֽל
18.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh also says that soldiers will take away some of your sons who will come forth from you, whom you will beget, and those sons will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon]

18.q: וּ⁠מִ⁠בָּנֶ֜י⁠ךָ אֲשֶׁ֨ר יֵצְא֧וּ מִמְּ⁠ךָ֛ אֲשֶׁ֥ר תּוֹלִ֖יד
18.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 8:12. Alternate translation: [some of the men of later generations who will descend from you, whose ancestor you will be]

18.q: וּ⁠מִ⁠בָּנֶ֜י⁠ךָ אֲשֶׁ֨ר יֵצְא֧וּ מִמְּ⁠ךָ֛ אֲשֶׁ֥ר תּוֹלִ֖יד
18.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [some of your actual biological descendants]

19.note: Hezekiah does not mean that the content of this message from Yahweh is objectively **good**. He means that he accepts and submits to what Yahweh has decided. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. The UST models one way to do that.
See how you translated the similar expression in 11:15. Alternate translation: [For he thought]

Hezekiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Is it not good, if peace and stability will be in my days?]

Hezekiah is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is good, since peace and stability will be in my days.]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **peace** and **stability**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [if my kingdom will be peaceful and stabile in my days]
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:36. Alternate translation: [during my lifetime]

20.q: וְ⁠יֶ֨תֶר דִּבְרֵ֤י חִזְקִיָּ֨הוּ֙ וְ⁠כָל־גְּב֣וּרָת֔⁠וֹ וַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֗ה אֶת־הַ⁠בְּרֵכָה֙ וְ⁠אֶת־הַ⁠תְּעָלָ֔ה וַ⁠יָּבֵ֥א אֶת־הַ⁠מַּ֖יִם הָ⁠עִ֑ירָ⁠ה הֲ⁠לֹא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־סֵ֛פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י הַ⁠יָּמִ֖ים לְ⁠מַלְכֵ֥י יְהוּדָֽה
20.note: In this verse and the next verse, the author is concluding the story of Hezekiah. To translate this verse, see how you translated the similar phrases in 1:18.

21.note: See how you translated the same expression in 8:24. Alternate translation: [And Hezekiah passed away] or [And Hezekiah died]
